title: Punjab's drug crisis
hook: families and gurdwaras are working to help young people out of addiction

segments.voice: Yesterday, caste, honestly, and your line was the gurus rejected it. Did you look at one bias of your own? Today, another hard subject, met the same way: with the lights on. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

A mother sits on the steps outside a gurdwara, holding her son's phone. He asked her to keep it. He's a few days into trying to stop, and he doesn't trust himself with the numbers saved inside it. Through the doors, kirtan is playing. A volunteer brings her a cup of tea and sits down next to her without asking a single question. In Punjab, families have been living stories like this one, and talking about them at kitchen tables, in songs, and in the gurdwara. Today isn't about blame. It's about the hands reaching in. Punjab's drug crisis.
screen: `A MOTHER HOLDS HER SON'S PHONE.` → `TEA, AND NO QUESTIONS.` → `THE HANDS REACHING IN.`

segments.voice: First, the hurt. Addiction in Punjab has reached into homes: a son, a cousin, a classmate, a neighbor's boy who used to play cricket in the lane. There are figures, and people argue about them. This lesson leaves them out, because behind every one of them is a person with a name. Second, what the Gurus said. In the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 554, Guru Amar Das describes what the false wine does: drinking it, a person loses their sense, can't tell their own from a stranger, and is pushed away from the Master. So, he says, don't drink this false wine at all, if it is in your power. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, carries the same teaching: Sikhs are asked to keep away from intoxicants, and the code names liquor, tobacco, opium and hemp among them. Third, the turn. The same salok doesn't stop at the warning. It speaks of a true wine, found by grace, by the one who meets the True Guru. The salok doesn't only take something away. It points to something to fill the empty place. Fourth, the hands. Families, doctors and sangats work on this together. Some gurdwaras and Sikh groups support recovery programs, sports for young people, and kirtan classes. Some sangats have learned to sit with a family instead of whispering about it. Shame keeps people hidden. A sangat that pulls a chair up to the table makes it easier to come out. That's today's line: help them out. Not lecture them out. Not shame them out. Help.
screen: `ADDICTION HAS REACHED INTO HOMES.` · `ANG 554: DON'T DRINK THE FALSE WINE.` · `A TRUE WINE, FOUND BY GRACE.` · `FAMILIES, DOCTORS AND SANGATS.` · then, large: `HELP THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on the steps. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Go back to the gurdwara steps from the story, and take the volunteer's place: a cup of tea in your hands, someone beside you who is carrying something heavy. It might be the mother. It might be someone you know, struggling with a drink, a drug, a screen, grief, or something they haven't told anyone. Don't speak. Don't fix anything. Just stay. Breathe in, and feel the warmth of the cup. Breathe out, and keep your place on the step. Sitting there is the whole job. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nasha. Intoxication, the addiction that has reached into Punjabi homes, with families, gurdwaras and doctors working to bring young people out of it. Today's word.

Your line: help them out. Today, offer one struggling person one small kindness, without a lecture attached. And if someone is in danger, get them to a doctor or emergency help first. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to avoid intoxicants. Some gurdwaras and Sikh organizations in Punjab and abroad support recovery work, youth programs and families facing addiction, alongside medical treatment.
